title: Dark Energy Camera Captures Circinus West Molecular Cloud
caption: The Circinus West molecular cloud, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Kosari (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A dark cloud creeps across this image like a shadow. It is the Circinus West molecular cloud, in the constellation Circinus, captured with the 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera (DECam), which NOIRLab ranks among the world's most powerful digital cameras.
Hidden behind the cloud's opaque edges is a stellar nursery. There, infant stars ignite out of cold, dense gas and dust, while outflows from the young stars fling leftover material back into space.

Molecular clouds are cold, dense regions of the gas between the stars, and the dust mixed through them blocks visible light from whatever lies inside or behind, which is why they look dark. Where the gas is dense enough, gravity pulls clumps together until they grow hot enough to shine as new stars. Young stars can also drive jets and outflows that carve into and stir up the surrounding cloud, shaping the nursery that formed them.
